query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Brief History of Blue

Blue is everywhere now: jeans, passports, corporate logos, police uniforms, hospital signs, social media apps, the sky in children’s drawings. But for much of human history, blue was strangely elusive. People saw the sea and the sky, of course, yet turning blue into a stable pigment, dye, symbol, and cultural idea took thousands of years.

The earliest important artificial blue was **Egyptian blue**, made in ancient Egypt more than four thousand years ago. It was a technological achievement: a synthetic pigment produced by heating sand, copper, lime, and an alkali. Egyptians used it on tomb paintings, statues, ceramics, and decorative objects. Because natural blue materials were rare, Egyptian blue carried associations of divinity, protection, rebirth, and the heavens.

In the ancient Mediterranean, blue did not always have the prestige it later gained. Greeks and Romans valued brilliant reds, purples, whites, and blacks more highly. Blue could seem foreign, barbarian, or unstable. Roman writers sometimes associated blue body paint with enemies at the edges of empire. Yet blue pigments and dyes still circulated through trade, especially from minerals and plants.

One of the most precious natural blues came from **lapis lazuli**, a deep blue stone mined mainly in Afghanistan and traded across Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. When ground into pigment, it produced **ultramarine**, whose name means “from beyond the sea.” In medieval Europe, ultramarine became one of the most expensive pigments available—sometimes more costly than gold. Artists reserved it for the most sacred or important figures, especially the Virgin Mary. Her blue robes helped transform blue into a colour of holiness, purity, and celestial authority.

At the same time, a more ordinary blue was produced from **woad**, a plant used in Europe to dye cloth. Later, **indigo**, imported from Asia and then cultivated under colonial systems in the Americas and elsewhere, became a major global dye. Indigo was richer and more efficient than woad, and its rise reshaped economies. But its history is also tied to forced labour, plantation agriculture, and imperial trade. The beauty of blue cloth often depended on brutal systems of production.

During the later Middle Ages and Renaissance, blue’s status rose dramatically. Kings adopted it in heraldry and clothing. The French monarchy used blue fields with golden fleurs-de-lis, strengthening the colour’s association with royalty and legitimacy. In Christian art, blue suggested heaven; in court culture, it suggested dignity; in clothing, it increasingly suggested refinement.

The scientific history of blue changed in the early modern period. Artists and chemists searched for cheaper, more reliable blues. In the early eighteenth century, **Prussian blue** was discovered accidentally in Berlin. It was intense, relatively affordable, and widely used in painting, printing, military uniforms, and later blueprints. It helped democratize a colour that had once depended on rare stones and expensive trade networks.

The nineteenth century brought more synthetic blues, including cobalt blue and artificial ultramarine. Industrial chemistry made blue increasingly accessible. Dyes transformed fashion, uniforms, household goods, and advertising. Blue became not only a sacred or aristocratic colour but an everyday one.

In the modern world, blue acquired new emotional and political meanings. It became the colour of trust, calm, order, and authority: police uniforms, business suits, bank logos, and international institutions all made use of it. It also became a colour of melancholy—“the blues”—linked to music, sadness, longing, and emotional depth. In politics, blue came to represent different things in different countries: conservatism in some places, liberalism or the left in others.

Perhaps the most democratic blue object is **denim**. Indigo-dyed workwear became the uniform of miners, labourers, cowboys, rebels, students, and eventually almost everyone. Blue jeans collapsed boundaries between class, gender, and nationality. What began as practical clothing became a global symbol of youth, freedom, informality, and mass culture.

Today, blue is often considered the world’s favourite colour. Its history helps explain why. It is ancient and modern, sacred and corporate, natural and synthetic, elite and ordinary. It has belonged to gods, queens, workers, soldiers, artists, and algorithms. Blue began as one of the hardest colours to capture; now it is one of the hardest to escape.
